name: Explosives 1.1 placard (Division 1.1)
meaning: Marks Division 1.1 explosives, which have a mass explosion hazard (for example, dynamite). It is a Table 1 material, so placards are required for any amount; never park within 5 feet of the traveled road or, except briefly for needs like fueling, within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, crowd or open fire.
commonsFile: File:1991 United States Hazmat Placard - Explosives 1.1.svg

name: Explosives 1.4 placard (Division 1.4)
meaning: Marks Division 1.4 explosives, which have only a minor explosion hazard (for example, ammunition). It is a Table 2 material: placards are required when the vehicle carries 1,001 pounds or more of Table 2 materials.
commonsFile: File:1991 United States Hazmat Placard - Explosives 1.4 - Blank.svg

name: Explosives 1.5 placard (Division 1.5, blasting agents)
meaning: Marks Division 1.5 very insensitive explosives, also called blasting agents. It is a Table 2 material: placards are required when the vehicle carries 1,001 pounds or more of Table 2 materials.
commonsFile: File:1991 United States Hazmat Placard - Explosives 1.5 - Blank.svg

name: Explosives 1.6 placard (Division 1.6)
meaning: Marks Division 1.6 extremely insensitive explosives (explosive devices). It is a Table 2 material: placards are required when the vehicle carries 1,001 pounds or more of Table 2 materials.
commonsFile: File:1991 United States Hazmat Placard - Explosives 1.6.svg

name: Flammable gas placard (Division 2.1)
meaning: Marks Division 2.1 flammable gases such as propane. It is a Table 2 material (1,001 pounds or more); never use flares around a tank used for flammable gas, loaded or empty, and never smoke within 25 feet of one.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Flammable Gas.svg

name: Non-flammable gas placard (Division 2.2)
meaning: Marks Division 2.2 non-flammable compressed gases such as helium. It is a Table 2 material: placards are required when the vehicle carries 1,001 pounds or more of Table 2 materials.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Non-Flammable Gas.svg

name: Oxygen placard (Division 2.2)
meaning: Used for compressed or refrigerated liquid oxygen, a Division 2.2 gas that also feeds fire. In domestic transportation it may be used in place of the NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard; Table 2 rules (1,001 pounds or more) apply.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Oxygen.svg

name: Poison gas placard (Division 2.3)
meaning: Marks Division 2.3 poisonous (toxic) gases; the current design reads INHALATION HAZARD with class 2 at the bottom. It is a Table 1 material, so placards are required for any amount.
commonsFile: File:1998 - United States Hazmat Placard - Inhalation Hazard - Class 2.svg

name: Poison inhalation hazard placard (Division 6.1)
meaning: Marks Division 6.1 poisons that are toxic to breathe (INHALATION HAZARD on the shipping paper or package). It is required for any amount (Table 1), in addition to any other placards the hazard class needs.
commonsFile: File:1998 - United States Hazmat Placard - Inhalation Hazard - Class 6.svg

name: Flammable liquid placard (Class 3)
meaning: Marks Class 3 flammable liquids such as gasoline. It is a Table 2 material (1,001 pounds or more, or any amount in bulk); never use flares around a Class 3 tank, loaded or empty, and never smoke within 25 feet.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Flammable.svg

name: Combustible liquid placard
meaning: Marks combustible liquids such as fuel oil (a category of its own, though the placard shows a 3). It is in Table 2; a FLAMMABLE placard may be used in its place on a cargo tank or portable tank.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Combustible.svg

name: Flammable solid placard (Division 4.1)
meaning: Marks Division 4.1 flammable solids (for example, wetted ammonium picrate). It is a Table 2 material; Class 4 loads must be in a closed cargo space or fully covered by a fire- and water-resistant tarp.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Flammable Solid.svg

name: Spontaneously combustible placard (Division 4.2)
meaning: Marks Division 4.2 materials that can catch fire on their own, such as white phosphorus. It is a Table 2 material; these loads need a vehicle with enough ventilation.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Spontaneously Combustible.svg

name: Dangerous when wet placard (Division 4.3)
meaning: Marks Division 4.3 materials that react dangerously with water, such as sodium. It is a Table 1 material, so placards are required for any amount; keep the load dry during loading, transit and unloading.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Dangerous When Wet.svg

name: Oxidizer placard (Division 5.1)
meaning: Marks Division 5.1 oxidizers such as ammonium nitrate. It is a Table 2 material; never smoke around oxidizers and do not carry them as an overhang or tailgate load.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Oxidizer.svg

name: Organic peroxide placard (Division 5.2)
meaning: Marks Division 5.2 organic peroxides such as methyl ethyl ketone peroxide (red top half, yellow bottom half). Type B temperature-controlled organic peroxide needs placards in any amount (Table 1); other organic peroxides are Table 2.
commonsFile: File:2007 - United States Hazmat Placard - Organic Peroxide.svg

name: Poison placard (Division 6.1)
meaning: Marks Division 6.1 poisonous (toxic) materials such as potassium cyanide that are not an inhalation hazard. It is a Table 2 material; never load POISON-labeled packages in the cab or sleeper or with food for people or animals.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Poison.svg

name: Radioactive placard (Class 7)
meaning: Marks Class 7 radioactive materials such as uranium. Any amount of packages with the Radioactive Yellow III label requires it (Table 1); the carrier must choose the safest route and show the driver the route plan.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Radioactive.svg

name: Corrosive placard (Class 8)
meaning: Marks Class 8 corrosives such as battery fluid. It is a Table 2 material; load breakable containers of corrosive liquid one by one, right side up, and never next to or above materials like Division 4.1 or Class 5.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Corrosive.svg

name: Class 9 placard (miscellaneous hazardous materials)
meaning: Marks Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous materials such as PCBs (seven black stripes on top, underlined 9). It is in Table 2, but a Class 9 placard is not required for domestic transportation.
commonsFile: File:1991 - United States Hazmat Placard - Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials.svg

name: Dangerous placard (mixed loads)
meaning: May be used instead of separate placards when a vehicle has 1,001 pounds or more of two or more Table 2 hazard classes. It cannot replace the class placard for 2,205 pounds or more of one class loaded at one place, and never replaces Table 1 placards; it is an option, not a requirement.
commonsFile: File:1977 United States Placard - Dangerous.svg
